questions.problem:
An environmental researcher is tracking the depth $d$, in meters, of a lake during a dry season. The following table shows the rate at which the depth is decreasing.

| **$t\,\text{(weeks)}$** | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ | $4$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${d}^{′}(t)\,\text{(meters/week)}$ | $-0.3$ | $-0.5$ | $-0.8$ | $-1.0$ |

At $t=2,$ the lake depth was $12$ meters. Use the tangent line approximation of $d$ at time $t=2$ to estimate the depth of the lake at $t=2.4.$ Do not round the answer.

The depth of the lake at $t=2.4$ weeks is estimated to be
{{field-1}}
meters.
questions.worked_solution:
The tangent line approximation of $d(t)$ at the point $a=2$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L(t) & =d(a)+{d}^{′}(a)(t-a) \\  & =d(2)+{d}^{′}(2)(t-2) \\  & =12+(-0.5)(t-2).\end{aligned}
$$

We can approximate $d(2.4)$ by evaluating the tangent line approximation at $t=2.4.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}d(2.4) & ≈L(2.4) \\  & =12+(-0.5)(2.4-2) \\  & =12+(-0.5)(0.4) \\  & =12-0.2 \\  & =11.8.\end{aligned}
$$

The depth of the lake at $t=2.4$ weeks is estimated to be $11.8$ meters.

questions.problem:
An engineer measures the amount of fuel $F$, in liters, remaining in a generator. The following table shows the rate at which fuel is being consumed.

| **$t\,\text{(hours)}$** | $2$ | $4$ | $6$ | $8$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${F}^{′}(t)\,\text{(liters/hour)}$ | $-3.1$ | $-3.5$ | $-4.0$ | $-4.4$ |

At $t=4,$ the generator contained $62$ liters of fuel. Use the tangent line approximation of $F$ at time $t=4$ to estimate the amount of fuel remaining at $t=4.6.$  Do not round the answer.

The amount of fuel remaining at $t=4.6$ hours is estimated to be
{{field-1}}
liters.
questions.worked_solution:
The tangent line approximation of $F(t)$ at the point $a=4$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L(t) & =F(a)+{F}^{′}(a)(t-a) \\  & =F(4)+{F}^{′}(4)(t-4) \\  & =62-3.5(t-4).\end{aligned}
$$

We can approximate $F(4.6)$ by evaluating the tangent line approximation at $t=4.6.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}F(4.6) & ≈L(4.6) \\  & =62-3.5(4.6-4) \\  & =62-3.5(0.6) \\  & =62-2.1 \\  & =59.9.\end{aligned}
$$

The amount of fuel remaining at $t=4.6$ hours is estimated to be $59.9$ liters.

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a) \\  & =f(1)+{f}^{′}(1)(x-1) \\  & =-4+2(x-1) \\  & =-4+2x-2 \\  & =2x-6.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Let $f$ be a function such that ${f}^{′}(x)=(2x-3)^{2}(x-1)^{4}$ and $f(0)=-2.$ Use the tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at $x=0$ to estimate the value of $f(1).$
questions.worked_solution:
The tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at the point $a=0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a) \\  & =f(0)+{f}^{′}(0)(x-0) \\  & =f(0)+{f}^{′}(0)x\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that $f(0)=-2,$ and since ${f}^{′}(x)==(2x-3)^{2}(x-1)^{4},$ then ${f}^{′}(0)==(2(0)-3)^{2}(0-1)^{4}=9.$ So, the tangent line approximation is given by

$$
L(x)=-2+9x.
$$

Now, we can approximate $f(1)$ by evaluating the tangent line approximation at $x=1.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1) & ≈L(1) \\  & =-2+9(1) \\  & =-2+9 \\  & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Let $f$ be a function such that ${f}^{′}(x)={x}^{2}(4x-9)$ and $f(1)=-2.$ Use the tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at $x=1$ to estimate the value of $f(1.5).$
questions.worked_solution:
The tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at the point $a=1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a) \\  & =f(1)+{f}^{′}(1)(x-1).\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that $f(1)=-2,$ and since ${f}^{′}(x)={x}^{2}(4x-9),$ then ${f}^{′}(1)={1}^{2}(4\cdot 1-9)=-5.$ So, the tangent line approximation is given by

$$
L(x)=-2-5(x-1).
$$

Now, we can approximate $f(1.5)$ by evaluating the tangent line approximation at $x=1.5.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1.5) & ≈L(1.5) \\  & =-2-5(1.5-1) \\  & =-2-5(0.5) \\  & =-2-2.5 \\  & =-4.5.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Let $f$ be a function such that ${f}^{′}(x)=2x$ and $f(2)=4.$ Use the tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at $x=2$ to estimate the value of $f(3).$
questions.worked_solution:
The tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at the point $a=2$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a) \\  & =f(2)+{f}^{′}(2)(x-2).\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that $f(2)=4,$ and since ${f}^{′}(x)=2x,$ then ${f}^{′}(2)=2(2)=4.$ So, the tangent line approximation is given by

$$
L(x)=4+4(x-2).
$$

Now, we can approximate $f(3)$ by evaluating the tangent line approximation at $x=3.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(3) & ≈L(3) \\  & =4+4(3-2) \\  & =4+4(1) \\  & =4+4 \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
The tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at the point $a=\frac{\pi }{6}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a) \\  & =f(\frac{\pi }{6})+{f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{6})(x-\frac{\pi }{6}).\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that $f(\frac{\pi }{6})=1,$ and since ${f}^{′}(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x,$ we have

$$
{f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{6})=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})=\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}.
$$

So, the tangent line approximation is given by

$$
L(x)=1+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}(x-\frac{\pi }{6}).
$$

Now, we can approximate $f(\frac{\pi }{5})$ by evaluating the tangent line approximation at $x=\frac{\pi }{5}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\frac{\pi }{5}) & ≈L(\frac{\pi }{5}) \\  & =1+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}(\frac{\pi }{5}-\frac{\pi }{6}) \\  & =1+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}\cdot \frac{\pi }{30} \\  & =1+\frac{\pi \sqrt{3}}{120}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Let $f$ be a function such that ${f}^{′}(x)={x}^{2}-4$ and $f(4)=13.$ Use the tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at $x=4$ to estimate the value of $f(3.5).$
questions.worked_solution:
The tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at the point $a=4$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a) \\  & =f(4)+{f}^{′}(4)(x-4).\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that $f(4)=13,$ and since ${f}^{′}(x)={x}^{2}-4,$ then ${f}^{′}(4)={4}^{2}-4=12.$ So, the tangent line approximation is given by

$$
L(x)=13+12(x-4).
$$

Now, we can approximate $f(3.5)$ by evaluating the tangent line approximation at $x=3.5.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(3.5) & ≈L(3.5) \\  & =13+12(3.5-4) \\  & =13+12(-0.5) \\  & =13-6 \\  & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing a Tangent Line Approximation and Classifying it as an Underestimate or Overestimate
questions.problem: The graph of the function $y=f(x)$ passes through $(3,-3)$ and is concave down on the interval $(1,4).$ If ${f}^{′}(3)=4,$ estimate the value of $f(3.2)$ using the tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at $x=3$ and determine whether the approximation is an underestimate or overestimate.
questions.worked_solution:
The tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at the point $a=3$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a) \\  & =f(3)+{f}^{′}(3)(x-3).\end{aligned}
$$

The function passes through the point $(3,-3),$ so we have $f(3)=-3.$ Also, we're told that ${f}^{′}(3)=4,$ so we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =-3+4(x-3) \\  & =-3+4x-12 \\  & =4x-15.\end{aligned}
$$

We can approximate $f(3.2)$ by evaluating the tangent line approximation at $x=3.2.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(3.2) & ≈L(3.2) \\  & =4(3.2)-15 \\  & =12.8-15 \\  & =-2.2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the function is concave down on the interval $(1,4),$ the linear approximation $L(x)$ is above the graph near $x=3,$ and therefore we have an overestimate.

questions.problem: The graph of the function $y=f(x)$ passes through $(-3,-4)$ and is concave down on the interval $(-4,-2).$ If ${f}^{′}(-3)=3,$ estimate the value of $f(-2.9)$ using the tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at $x=-3$ and determine whether the approximation is an underestimate or overestimate.
questions.worked_solution:
The tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at the point $a=-3$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a) \\  & =f(-3)+{f}^{′}(-3)(x+3).\end{aligned}
$$

The graph of the function passes through the point $(-3,-4),$ so we have $f(-3)=-4.$ Also, we're told that ${f}^{′}(-3)=3,$ so we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =-4+3(x+3) \\  & =-4+3x+9 \\  & =3x+5.\end{aligned}
$$

We can approximate $f(-2.9)$ by evaluating the tangent line approximation at $x=-2.9.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-2.9) & ≈L(-2.9) \\  & =3(-2.9)+5 \\  & =-8.7+5 \\  & =-3.7.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the function is concave down on the interval $(-4,-2),$ the linear approximation $L(x)$ is above the graph near $x=-3,$ and therefore we have an overestimate.

questions.problem: Given that the tangent line approximation to the function $f(x)$ at $x=\sqrt{2}$ overestimates the values of the function in the neighborhood of $x=\sqrt{2},$ which of the following must be true?
questions.worked_solution:
Since the tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at $x=\sqrt{2}$ overestimates the values of the function, we have

$$
L(x)>f(x),
$$

that is, the line $L(x)$ must be above the graph of $f(x)$ near the point  $x=\sqrt{2}.$

Therefore, the function must be concave down in the neighborhood of $x=\sqrt{2}.$

choices.value: $f(x)$ is concave down in the neighborhood of $x=\sqrt{2}$
$f(x)$ is concave up in the neighborhood of $x=\sqrt{2}$

answer_fields.correct_value: $f(x)$ is concave down in the neighborhood of $x=\sqrt{2}$

questions.problem: The graph of the function $y=f(x)$ passes through $(2,3)$ and is concave up on the interval $(0,3).$ If ${f}^{′}(2)=-1,$ estimate the value of $f(2.2)$ using the tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at $x=2$ and determine whether the approximation is an underestimate or overestimate.
questions.worked_solution:
The tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at the point $a=2$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a) \\  & =f(2)+{f}^{′}(2)(x-2).\end{aligned}
$$

The function passes through the point $(2,3),$ so we have $f(2)=3.$ Also, we're told that ${f}^{′}(2)=-1,$ so we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =3+(-1)(x-2) \\  & =3-(x-2).\end{aligned}
$$

We can approximate $f(2.2)$ by evaluating the tangent line approximation at $x=2.2.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2.2) & ≈L(2.2) \\  & =3-(2.2-2) \\  & =3-0.2 \\  & =2.8.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the function is concave up on the interval $(0,3),$ the linear approximation $L(x)$ is below the graph near $x=2,$ and therefore we have an underestimate.

The tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at the point $a=2$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a) \\  & =f(2)+{f}^{′}(2)(x-2).\end{aligned}
$$

The graph of the function passes through the point $(2,1),$ so we have $f(2)=1.$ Also, we're told that ${f}^{′}(2)=1.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =1+1(x-2) \\  & =x-1.\end{aligned}

Now, we can approximate $f(1.6)$ by evaluating the tangent line approximation at $x=1.6.$ We get

canonical_examples.problem: Suppose that $f(-2) = 0$ and $f'(-2)=2.$ Estimate the value of $f(-1.8)$ using the tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at $x=-2.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The tangent line approximation to $f(x)$ at the point $a=-2$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a) \\  & =f(-2)+{f}^{′}(-2)(x-(-2)) \\  & =0+2(x+2) \\  & =2(x+2).\end{aligned}
$$

We can approximate $f(-1.8)$ by evaluating the tangent line approximation at $x=-1.8.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-1.8) & ≈L(-1.8) \\  & =2(-1.8+2) \\  & =2(0.2) \\  & =0.4.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Let $g$ be a function such that $g'(x) =\sqrt{x}$ and $g(4) = 3.$ Using the tangent line approximation of $g(x)$ at $x=4,$ estimate the value of $g(3.6).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The tangent line approximation to $g(x)$ at the point $a=4$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =g(a)+{g}^{′}(a)(x-a) \\  & =g(4)+{g}^{′}(4)(x-4).\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that $g(4)=3,$ and since $g'(x)=\sqrt{x},$ then $g'(4)=\sqrt{4}=2.$ So, the tangent line approximation is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =3+2(x-4).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can approximate $g(3.6)$ by evaluating the tangent line approximation at $x=3.6.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}g(3.6) & ≈L(3.6) \\  & =3+2(3.6-4) \\  & =3+2(-0.4) \\  & =3-0.8 \\  & =2.2.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: The graph of the function $y=f(x)$ passes through $(-2,-5)$ and is concave down on the interval $(-\infty,0).$ If $f'(-2)=3$, estimate the value of $f(-2.3)$ using the tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at $x=-2$ and determine whether the approximation is an underestimate or overestimate.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The tangent line approximation to $f(x)$ at the point $a=-2$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a) \\  & =f(-2)+{f}^{′}(-2)(x-(-2)) \\  & =f(-2)+{f}^{′}(-2)(x+2).\end{aligned}
$$

The function passes through the point $(-2,-5),$ so we have $f(-2)=-5.$ Also, we're told that $f'(-2)=3,$ so we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =-5+3(x+2).\end{aligned}
$$

We can approximate $f(-2.3)$ by evaluating the tangent line approximation at $x=-2.3.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-2.3) & ≈L(-2.3) \\  & =-5+3(-2.3+2) \\  & =-5+3(-0.3) \\  & =-5-0.9 \\  & =-5.9.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the function is concave down on the interval $(-\infty,0)$, the linear approximation $L(x)$ is above the graph near $x=-2,$ and therefore we have an overestimate.
